title: A Function on the Join Column Kills the Seek
description: Wrapping a join column in UPPER() makes the predicate non-sargable and scans; compare the column bare and fix case at the data layer.
narrative:
## Scenario
A "defensive" join wraps the reference code in `UPPER()` to guard against case differences: `ON UPPER(o.CustomerRef) = c.Ref`. The data is already uppercase, so it changes no results — but it turns a one-customer lookup into a full scan of 300,000 orders.

## Why it's slow
`IX_Orders_CustomerRef` indexes the raw column value. Wrapping it in `UPPER(o.CustomerRef)` means the engine can't match the *stored* value to an index entry — it must compute `UPPER()` on **every row** first. The join predicate is no longer **sargable**, so the seek collapses into an **Index Scan** of the whole Orders table.

## What to look for
- An Index Scan of Orders instead of a per-customer seek.
- The join predicate wraps the indexed column in a function (`UPPER`, `LOWER`, `LTRIM`, `CAST`, arithmetic...).

## The concept
Never wrap an indexed column in a function inside a join or WHERE — it defeats the index. Compare the column **bare**: `ON o.CustomerRef = c.Ref`. If case really is inconsistent, fix it at the data layer (a consistent collation, or normalize on write) rather than with a per-row `UPPER()` that silently disables every index on the column.
startingQuery:
SELECT o.OrderId, o.Total
FROM dbo.Orders o
JOIN dbo.Customers c ON UPPER(o.CustomerRef) = c.Ref
WHERE c.CustomerId = 42;
hints: The join wraps o.CustomerRef in UPPER(), so the stored index values can't be matched directly -- the index is scanned, not seeked.
A function on the indexed column makes the predicate non-sargable. The data is already uppercase, so the UPPER() is pure overhead.
Compare the column bare: ON o.CustomerRef = c.Ref.
